en: And afterward to die—
I stood crying out and weeping.
My father Esen Khan—
Whether he had some sacred power,
I marvel at it now.
“Ah, my foal, Kongurbay,
His father was a lesser khan.
That same Azyz Khan
Had yearned for a single child.
His spring flowing down from the river,
His long-awaited lamp.
We talked a lot,
Azyz Khan's Kan-Zhaylak—
You have seized that land.
He too was a khan's son;
You too were a khan's son.
Your fathers were born as equals;
I see you two as equal brothers.”
When Esen Khan said this,
Kongurbay grew furious,
Taking offense at Esen Khan.
No sooner had this happened,
Before a word could be spoken,
Before an eye could open and close,
The guards my father had appointed,
Sixty Chinese and forty Sibe,
Came rushing in bewildered.
Then a Sibe said this:
“My khan, my lord, a report before you:
A man has come to the door,
Tall and broad-shouldered,
An outstanding champion and a lion,
With the look of a hungry lion.
The mount beneath him,
He has his horse Aysarala;
The whole wide world
He has the strength to lay it all waste.
His whole body is buttoned up;
All his rounded form
Is adorned with blue iron.
A banner flutters in his hand;
A camel-cleaving sword and battle-axe
Flash upon his arm.
His blazing eyes shine;
His renown is great, his look fearsome.
No one who attacks him stays alive.
If strife and trouble rise from Beijing,
No such hero is born among mortals.
A head taller than the giant Mangkysh,
So much taller than the giant Kutan,
Greater in girth than Zholoy Khan,
Higher still than Ylama,
A hero beyond Ezkara,
More imposing than Boronchu,
Far above the giant Delpi,
This much above Muzkindik,
Far above the giant Tiken.
There is simply no such soul;
No mortal who faces him escapes unharmed.
No mortal can come against him;
No one can stand in his way.
Broad-chested, with an ample breast,
Majestic, with dark eyes—
Lord Esenkan, I say this fearing you!
Some marvel has come upon us;
His appearance is unlike other men,
His dread presence unlike any mortal's.
He has readied armor and weapons.
The mount beneath him,
Sarala, as though lit by the moon,
Has hoe-like hooves and broad haunches,
A horse to ride into battle.
A Karabair horse, with brazen forelegs,
A mount to ride into combat—
My khan, he will bring great calamity upon your people.
High-backed, yet low in stature,
Driven over hills, he never tires.
Among beasts there is no such horse;
Among men there is no such soul.”
When he heard this,
My khan father came outside.
When he saw Esenkan's face,
Without paying homage or bowing his head,
God had utterly struck him:
“Of the Chinese people of forty khans,
Give me one khanate,” he said,
And stood asking for a khanate.
My father Esenkan
Did not agree to what he said;
Of the forty tribes of Chinese and Machin,
He gave him no khanate.
My father Esen said:
“Son, you have not outgrown childhood;
You have not reached twenty years.
Wisdom has not settled in your breast;
Your time to become khan has not come.
Your strength has not fully matured;
You have not outgrown childhood.”
When my father said this,
Almam took offense over the khanate;
He jerked and shook himself,
And raged like a lion.
His double-edged Zulpukor
He drew and made ready.
Blue flame came from his mouth;
It darted aside with a whirring rush.
His mighty teeth, broad as gates,
Rattled like grains of millet.
He lunged like a lion, eyes ablaze;
His thirst for blood seized him in earnest.
His mouth and face murmured;
All about his mouth and nose
Twitched beyond his control.
Seeing Almambet's appearance,
Esenkan started in alarm;
Unable to withstand his wrath,
He fled inside the palace.
Then your dear Alake
Turned Sarala's head,
And outside Esenkan's door
Kept watch for nine days.
When I saw Almambet,
My heart burned like fire;
Longing to see that noble one's face,
I watched with desperate yearning.
Rejoicing at the sight of him,
I bounded and sprang like a roe deer.
If snow falls upon the dark earth,
Look at the snow, then at my skin;
If blood falls upon the snow,
Look at the blood, then at my face.
In a crimson dress, with a slender waist,
I, your mother's sworn sister, flitted there,
With a thimble-small mouth and camel-calf eyes,
Beautiful, with playful, languishing eyes.
Turning aside and stepping away,
Before my valiant one
I appeared, flitting into view.
Valiant Almam, that noble lion,
Struck Sarala once upon the flank,
Reached round and caught me by the neck,
And laid his hand upon my breast.
Almambet said this,
Something no man had heard:
“Your father, that fool Esenkan—
Let me bring him to his end as well.
Damn you, heed my words;
Let me take you away as my bride.
With clamorous Beijing and Chynchy Khan
Let me raise a mighty quarrel;
Let me plunge in and fight six months,
And take you for my bride.
Your father begrudges his khanate;
Let me bring him to his end this way.
Damn you, please heed my words;
Let me take you away as my bride!
Of the countless Chinese,
Even if they give me a general's hat button, I will not take it.
Heed my words now,”
He said, standing thus,
And making this commotion.
Your dear Alake had not yet mounted a horse;
He had not yet become known as Almambet;
Manas had not yet existed then;
He had not yet turned and entered the faith.
Then I spoke a word,
A harsh word that troubled his heart.
I shook off his hand in anger.
From the first, I, poor soul, was firmly Muslim;
I called him to the Muslim faith,
And told him to become a Muslim.
Before your dear Alake
I myself came shining,
And urged him to become a Muslim.
“One to gather me if I am scattered,
Hear my plea and heed my words,
My beloved fellow believer.
Forsake your father: he is an unbeliever;
Your faith is nearer than your father.
Forsake your people: they are unbelievers;
Your faith is nearer than your people.
Your Chinese homeland is unbelieving;
Your faith is nearer than your homeland.
Understand these sorrowful words;
Do not grieve me, Almam; heed my words.
This world is a merchant;
Though you go on thundering,
One day you will die at last.
Tomorrow, on the Day of Judgment,
What answer will you give?
One who knows the faith is a hero;
One who knows it not is an unbeliever.”
Then I said this:
“Say, ‘In the name of God,’
And will you heed me, Almambet?
God is one, the Quran is true—
Do you know this, Almambet?
My faith lies with the Muslims.
I saw a saint in my dream,
And stood as your bride.
If you think, Almam, heed my words;
Understand these words I have spoken.
Ancestral spirits were born pure,
I may devote myself to Allah,
You were a son of light,
I, being Ur's daughter,
On God's blessed day,
On Friday's Night of Power,
I saw a wondrous, lovely dream:
United when thumb-small,
Joined when tiny as a louse,
I saw such a happy thing.”
Thus I spoke a word,
The lion who had gone to the next world—
I planted a troubling word in his heart.
When I said this,
His swift steed Aisarala
He could not urge forward, but wandered in distress.
That was the beginning of our promise;
Thus we went on together.
This trouble came in the end;
Thus we were wed.
Because of wretched, hapless me,
Muzburchak and Kokcho Khan died,
And all who encountered it died.
Your khan father Manas, that bloodthirsty lion,
Went into Kakan and returned,
Bereft of his valiant men.
Beijing, six months away,
He called a six-day journey.
Beijing, untouched by the Holy One,
He called an army in motley shirts.
Beijing, with its formidable mountain paths,
He attacked from the heights,
And all his valiant men
He let the Chinese take as martyrs.
Beijing, twelve months away,
The Chinese ten days away,
He deemed more abject than other mortals.
Beijing, where the Prophet would not tread,
He attacked from the front,
And all his heroes
He let the Chinese take as gifts.
Going into Kakan and returning,
Your khan father lost his valiant men.
When Akkula fell to a bullet,
When your Alake passed away a martyr,
There is an ember left in this world:
From Almam, who went before,
Left to me as a gift,
There is a six-year-old child.
When we remember Almambet,
We blaze and burn with grief.
Behind him is six-year-old Kulchoro;
We go on taking strength from him.”
Your mother's sworn sister Burulcha
